o: Heavenly Father, I thank You for this new day You give me. Before the rushing begins, I want to pause a moment before You and acknowledge that You are my Creator, my Sustainer and my greatest treasure. Thank You for the air I breathe, for the night's rest and for Your mercy that is renewed every morning.

Lord, You know the thoughts that trouble me, the questions I do not know how to answer and the desires that sometimes lead me away from Your path. Today I give You my heart, weary of seeking peace in the wrong places. Quiet me, as a child is quieted in his mother's arms. Teach me to rest in Your love and not to depend on what happens or on what others say about me.

Guide my steps from the very first moment. Help me speak with kindness, work with diligence and look at every person with Your eyes. If I go wrong, remind me that Your grace reaches me and that I can always return to You. Take care of my family, my friends and those going through pain today. At the end of this day, may I be able to say that You were with me at every step. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 13, in the year 354, a boy named Augustine was born in Thagaste, in North Africa. His mother, Monica, was a woman of sincere faith who prayed for him constantly. Augustine grew up with a brilliant mind, but he sought happiness in glory, in pleasures and in fashionable ideas, and his heart remained empty.

With the years, he came to Milan as a teacher of rhetoric. There he listened to the preaching of Bishop Ambrose, and his questions grew deeper. At the end of the summer of 386, tormented inside, he heard the voice of a child repeating: “Take up and read.” He opened the book of the apostle Paul's letters, and his eyes fell on Romans 13:13-14, which calls us to put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Augustine later recounted, in his Confessions, that at the end of that reading the light of peace filled his heart and the darkness of doubt dispersed.

On the eve of Easter in the year 387, he was baptized in Milan by Ambrose. Later he returned to Africa, became bishop of Hippo and wrote works that have nourished the faith of believers for more than fifteen hundred years. He died in Hippo on August 28 of the year 430. In the first pages of his Confessions, he left a very well-known sentence: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

His story teaches us that no one is too far for God to reach, and that the prayers of a faithful mother do not fall into the void. What Augustine sought for years in so many places, he finally found in Jesus Christ.
m.c: Today, may you walk with a quiet heart, knowing that God sustains you at every step. What you cannot settle, leave in his hands, and what is yours to do, do with joy. His grace will accompany you from this morning until the coming of night.
m: Augustine sought for years what only God could give him. Today something similar happens to us: we believe peace will come with an achievement, a purchase, the approval of others or the end of a problem. And when those things arrive, the emptiness is still there. It is not that those things are bad, but they were made to be gifts, not to occupy God's place in the heart.

The psalmist expresses it with a very tender image in Psalm 131: “I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother.” It is not the calm of one who understands everything, but of one who trusts the one who carries him. And Psalm 127 reminds us that it is vain to rise early and fret in anxiety, for God gives sleep to those he loves. You do not have to carry this day all by yourself.

Here is a practical application for today. When you feel that restlessness that pushes you to run, stop for a minute, breathe deeply and say in a low voice: “Lord, I rest in you.” Before looking at your phone, read a verse and think about it during the morning. And if you catch yourself wanting to fill an emptiness with something, ask yourself sincerely what your soul really needs at that moment.

Think also of Monica. She did not immediately see her son's change, but she kept praying faithfully. Today you can do the same for someone you love who seems far from God. Place their name before the Lord, without growing weary. God works in his own time, and no prayer made in faith is lost.

t.t: The One Who Returned to Give Thanks
o: Lord Jesus, as I close this day, I want to do what that man who returned did: go back to Your feet and give You thanks. Thank You for life, for health, for the roof that shelters me and for today's food. Thank You for the people who helped me and for those who put up with me in my difficult days. Every good thing, great or small, is a gift of Your mercy. Today I do not want to be among those who go their own way, but among those who return to You with a full heart.

Forgive me for the times I received Your blessings and went on my way without remembering You. Often I ask insistently and give thanks in haste. Teach me to have a heart that returns. Thank You for the prayers You have answered, and also for those still awaiting an answer, for I know that Your timing is perfect and that Your love does not fail.

Now I give You the burdens of the day: the unsettled matters, the worries for my own and the weariness I carry. Take care of my family while they sleep, heal the sick and console those who are alone. May my rest be quiet and may I wake tomorrow with a song of gratitude. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: Jesus, on his way to Jerusalem, was passing between Samaria and Galilee. As he entered a village, ten lepers met him and stood at a distance. Leprosy forced them to live apart from their family and community, and to cry out a warning that they were unclean. They were men alone, sick and without human hope, united by the same misfortune. No one was waiting for them in any home, and no one came near them.

They lifted up their voices and said: “Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!” When Jesus saw them, he said to them: “Go and show yourselves to the priests.” They had not yet been healed, but they obeyed and set out. And as they went, they were cleansed. Imagine the joy of feeling the skin renew and the disease disappear in the middle of the road. Their faith showed itself on the way, before they saw the miracle.

One of them, seeing that he was healed, turned back, glorifying God with a loud voice, and fell on his face at Jesus' feet, giving him thanks. And he was a Samaritan, that is, a foreigner. Jesus asked: “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the other nine? Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?”

Then he said to him: “Rise and go your way; your faith has made you well.” All ten received healing, but only one received in addition the encounter with the Healer. Gratitude brought him back to the source of the good. This story invites us, at the end of every day, not to go our own way, but to return to Jesus with a grateful heart and say to him simply: thank you, Lord, for all you have given me. May this also be our habit every night.
t.c: Thank you for this day, which was a gift even if it did not look like one. Lay before the Lord what weighs on you and receive the rest that only he can give. May his love cradle you tonight and may his goodness wake you renewed.
m: Ending the day with gratitude changes the way we rest. It is easy to remember what was lacking, what went wrong or what bothered us, and to forget what we received. The ten lepers were healed, but only one came back. We do not know why the other nine did not return; perhaps they were happy, busy or hurrying to do what Jesus had told them. What is certain is that only one stopped to give thanks.

Notice what this man received by returning. The others were cleansed, but to him Jesus said: “Your faith has made you well.” Gratitude opened the door to a deeper encounter with the Lord. Giving thanks is not merely courtesy: it is acknowledging where what we have comes from, and it brings us closer to God and quiets the heart.

Psalm 107 begins by inviting us to praise the LORD because he is good and his steadfast love endures forever, and asks the redeemed to say so. You are one of them. Before sleeping, make a simple list of three good things from today: a person, a detail, an unexpected help. It does not matter how small they are.

Then say them aloud before God, one by one, and end with a “thank you, Lord.” If you can, thank someone tomorrow as well with a word or a message. When we learn to return and give thanks, weariness weighs less, burdens grow lighter and sleep comes with more peace.
